name: Elevated head sleeping / wedge pillow

lead: A wedge pillow or bed risers keep the head above the body while you sleep. Users raise their head to wake with a less puffy face, especially around the eyes.

The chain is simple: with the head raised, less fluid pools in the face while lying flat, so there is less morning puffiness. Head-of-bed elevation is an established lifestyle measure for reflux, and reference sources suggest it may limit fluid shifting around the eyes. No trial has tested it for facial appearance.

paras: Users place a foam wedge under the upper body or put risers under the head end of the bed and sleep that way nightly. It takes a few nights to adjust to, and it is often combined with low evening salt and alcohol.
Low risk. Some people get neck or back discomfort or slide down the wedge, and a wedge that raises only the head can bend the neck.

angle.text: Sleeping with the head raised on a wedge or risers keeps fluid from pooling in the face overnight, so users wake with less puffiness. Head-of-bed elevation is an established measure for reflux, and its effect on facial puffiness has not been tested.

lead: Sleeping with the head raised, using a wedge pillow, stacked pillows or blocks under the head of the bed, is a way people try to wake up with a less puffy face. Looksmaxxing and skincare communities say that keeping the head above the body overnight limits fluid pooling around the eyes and cheeks, so the face looks more defined in the morning. [1]

Wikipedia's article on periorbital puffiness notes that eye swelling is typically most noticeable right after waking, that lying flat lets fluid shift toward the face, and that elevating the head is a commonly suggested way to limit the pooling. [1] The same article lists other contributors, such as salt-heavy meals, alcohol, allergies, poor sleep and ageing. [1]

Head-of-bed elevation is also an established non-drug measure for gastro-oesophageal reflux, and wedge pillows have been tested in trials for that purpose. [2][3] No published trial has tested a wedge pillow for facial puffiness or appearance. Head-up sleeping has also been studied in obstructive sleep apnea, where a 2025 multicenter observational study measured breathing during sleep at a 30-degree head-of-bed angle.[4]
infobox: Foam wedge pillow, stacked pillows, bed risers, adjustable base

paras: A wedge pillow is a triangular foam cushion that slopes the upper body. Wikipedia lists it among orthopedic pillows and notes that wedge pillows are mainly used to relieve acid reflux and GERD symptoms during sleep, though they are multipurpose. [5] Other ways to achieve the same slope include blocks under the head-end bed legs and adjustable beds. [2]

Wedges are also used for comfort. On T Nation's training forum, members have suggested a wedge to support the head and shoulders for side sleepers with shoulder discomfort, and one reported wedging a pillow behind their back to avoid crushing a lower shoulder. [6][7]

Common forms are a one-piece foam wedge placed under the upper body, a stack of ordinary pillows, risers or blocks under the head-end legs of the bed frame, and adjustable bases that tilt the mattress. Wikipedia's reflux article describes raising the head of the bed on 6-inch blocks as one lifestyle measure, and notes the same advice is given during pregnancy.[8] Wedges that support only the head can bend the neck forward, whereas ones that slope the whole torso keep the spine in one line; this difference is a design point rather than something the studies compare.[2]

While upright, gravity pulls fluid toward the lower body. Lying flat removes that pull, and Wikipedia says this lets fluid move toward the face, which is why puffiness is most obvious on waking. [1] Elevating the head is described there as a way to limit the pooling around the eyes. [1]

Researchers have measured a related effect in the eye. A 2014 prospective, nonrandomised comparison of 30 patients (15 with glaucoma, 15 without) in a sleep laboratory found nocturnal intraocular pressure was on average 1.51 mm Hg lower at a 20-degree head-up position on a wedge pillow than lying flat, an 8 to 9 percent reduction. [9] This shows that the position changes fluid-related pressures in the head, though it measured eye pressure rather than appearance.

Wikipedia's article on sleep positions says raising the head lowers oesophageal acid exposure and acid clearance time, and notes that positional therapy that discourages back sleeping may reduce snoring.[10] The same article reports that positional obstructive sleep apnea, which improves when back sleeping is avoided, accounts for an estimated 56 to 75 percent of obstructive sleep apnea cases.[10]

In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the wedge is paired with other depuffing habits, such as lower evening salt and alcohol intake, cold compresses and facial massage in the morning. Wikipedia lists cold compresses and diet adjustment alongside head elevation as ways to manage puffiness. [1]

A 2021 systematic review of head-of-bed elevation for reflux screened 1,206 records and included five trials with 228 patients (two with bed blocks, one with a wedge pillow, two with both). All five were judged at high risk of performance bias and the trials were too varied for meta-analysis, but the four that reported reflux symptoms found improvement with elevation; a high-quality crossover trial showed a clinically important reduction in symptom scores at 6 weeks. [2]

A 2026 noninferiority randomised trial in 24 patients with persistent nocturnal reflux despite morning PPI compared adding a wedge pillow with adding an evening PPI for 4 weeks. At week 4 symptom questionnaire scores were 30.0 in the wedge group and 36.3 in the twice-daily PPI group. [3] A separate 2025 randomised trial of 256 patients tested an ergonomic wedge pillow during prone ERCP and found less next-day neck pain (19% vs 30%). [11]

A 2025 prospective multicenter study enrolled 30 people with obstructive sleep apnea and 30 healthy controls and recorded polysomnography supine, with the bed head raised 30 degrees and on the side. In the apnea group the apnea-hypopnea index fell from 25.7 supine to 17.8 with head elevation, and to 14.8 on the side; sleep efficiency rose from 73.0 to 79.0 percent with elevation, and half of the apnea patients had at least a 50 percent reduction in the index.[4] Better sleep is itself one of the factors Wikipedia lists among contributors to puffy-looking eyes, which is how some users link sleep-position aids to morning appearance.[1]

Wedge use is generally low-risk. Wikipedia's overview of orthopedic pillows notes that side sleeping puts pressure on shoulders and arms and that back sleeping may favour snoring and back pain, which is why pillow shape and support matter for comfort. [5] Persistent or severe facial swelling can indicate an underlying condition and warrants medical evaluation, according to Wikipedia. [1]

Reflux-related guidance on head elevation distinguishes a sloped torso from simply stacking pillows under the head, and users with neck or shoulder problems describe tailoring the slope to comfort.[2][6] Wikipedia's puffiness article lists allergies as the most common cause of eyelid swelling and several medical conditions among causes, so a sudden or lasting change in swelling is generally evaluated by a clinician.[1]
No studies found for facial puffiness or appearance.
Related trials exist for reflux (five trials in a 2021 review; a 2026 noninferiority trial), for neck pain after ERCP, and for nocturnal intraocular pressure at 20-degree head-up. [2][3][9][11]

lore.intro: Elevated sleeping is discussed in depuffing and sleep routines, and on T Nation mostly as a comfort aid for lifters. [6][7]
